Tell me in about 200 words why people in India are switching to UPI, with a short list of 3 reasons
9:55 AM

UPI has become India's default way to pay because it makes a bank transfer as quick as sending a text. You scan a code or enter a number, type your PIN, and the money moves from your bank account to theirs in seconds, at any hour, even on holidays.

Here are the three main reasons people are switching:

It's quick and usually free. Paying a friend, a shop or a bill normally costs nothing, and the money arrives at once. There's no waiting, no queue and no hunting for change.
It works almost everywhere. From a roadside tea stall to a big online store, one printed QR code is enough. Shopkeepers don't need a card machine, just a phone.
One app, any bank. You can link several accounts and pay anyone, whichever bank or UPI app they use. Nobody is locked into one provider.

Trust and habit do the rest. Once your local vendors accept UPI, carrying cash starts to feel like extra work. Banks, phone makers and the government have all pushed it, and the simple PIN steps make it easy even for first-time smartphone users. That's why a ₹10 payment for chai now feels as normal as a big transfer.
